title: Luther on vocation
hook: Luther taught that ordinary work, a milkmaid's or a cobbler's, can be a holy calling

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saint Benedict's monk's day in three, prayer, work and reading. Your line was idleness is the enemy of the soul. Did your three blocks hold? Today, a man who left the monastery. Day eight hundred ninety-one.
screen: `IDLENESS IS THE ENEMY OF THE SOUL.`

segments.voice: A cobbler hammers a heel onto a boot. A smith pumps the bellows. A farmer walks behind the plow. Ask a churchgoer in their town who has a calling from God, and the answer might point up the hill, to the monastery, to the priest at the altar. Then a monk named Martin Luther, a teacher of the Bible in Germany, starts saying something that sounds almost backward. The cobbler at his bench, he says, is doing God's work too. Not after hours. In the shoes. Today's word is the one he argued about.
screen: `A COBBLER, A SMITH, A FARMER.` → `WHO HAS A CALLING?` → `IN THE SHOES.`

segments.voice: Vocation. A calling. First, the argument. Luther objected to the idea that people in religious orders stood on a higher spiritual level than everyone else. In an open letter to the German nobility, he wrote that a cobbler, a smith and a farmer each has the work and office of his trade, and yet all of them are consecrated priests and bishops, through baptism. The spiritual life doesn't live in one building. Second, the verse he leaned on. Paul writes, in the King James Bible, "Let every man abide in the same calling wherein he was called." Luther read calling there to include a person's ordinary station: parent, servant, ruler, maker of things. Third, the milkmaid. A line often credited to Luther says that God himself milks the cows through the vocation of the milkmaid. It's hard to find those exact words in his writings, so treat it as a saying people pass on in his name. But it catches what he taught: the daily work that feeds and clothes and serves your neighbor is where God is at work. Fourth, what Christians made of it. Lutheran and other Protestant churches built on this idea of vocation. Catholic teaching today also speaks of the vocation of lay people in ordinary work and family life, alongside the calling to priesthood and religious life. Churches say it in their own ways and their own words. And the idea has traveled outside churches too. Someone who never thinks about Luther may still ask: what if this job, this shift, this kitchen, is more than a way to pay rent? What if it's a calling?
screen: `NO HIGHER RUNG FOR THE CLOISTER.` · `ABIDE IN THE SAME CALLING.` · `GOD MILKS THE COWS, IT'S SAID.` · `CHURCHES SAY IT THEIR OWN WAY.` · then, large: `VOCATION.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Luther read calling to include a person's station: parent, servant, ruler, maker of things. Name your own stations, one at a time. Maybe son or daughter. Parent. Coworker. Neighbor. Student. Patient. Friend. Let the list be as long as it is. Now choose the one that feels least holy, the one you'd never think to call a calling. Stay with it. Picture one ordinary moment in it today. You don't have to call it holy. Just let it count as yours. If you pray, you can bring that person and your work into your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Vocation. A calling. Luther argued that ordinary work, the cobbler's and the farmer's, can be a holy calling, not only the priest's or the monk's. Today's word.
Your line: my calling. Today, see your job as a calling. Take the station that felt least holy, and do one ordinary task in it as if you'd been called to it. Day eight hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Lutheran and other Protestant churches teach vocation as serving God and neighbor in ordinary work and family life; Catholic teaching also speaks of the vocation of lay people alongside priesthood and religious life.

fork.setup: you're a cobbler in Luther's town. you want to serve God better. Luther's teaching says…
options: close the shop and join a monastery.
your trade is already a calling: serve your neighbor through it.
give your earnings to the church and stop working.
fork.reveal: Luther wrote that the cobbler, the smith and the farmer each has the work and office of his trade, and all are consecrated priests. the shop is the calling.

trapdoor: what you thought: a vocation is a career path, or a priest's call.
what it means: for Luther, any ordinary work that serves your neighbor can be a holy calling.
what a scholar hears: Luther read Paul's 'abide in the same calling' to include a person's station in life, and argued against a higher rung for the cloister.

notes: The 'Open letter to the German nobility' paraphrase (cobbler, smith, farmer each has the work and office of his trade, all consecrated priests and bishops) should be checked against the text; no year given.
The milkmaid saying is presented as attributed and hard to find in Luther's writings; a scholar should confirm that framing.
Luther's reading of 1 Corinthians 7:20 (Beruf) is summarized without the German word to avoid an etymology claim.
'Lutheran and other Protestant churches built on this idea' uses 'many'; a Keeper may prefer 'other'. Catholic lay vocation phrasing (no council or date named) should be checked by a Catholic Keeper.
Hook calls Luther 'a teacher of the Bible in Germany'; no dates given.
Editor: practice and carry no longer repeat day 879's 'follow it outward: who uses what you do' angle; they now name one's own stations (Luther's reading of calling) and pick the least holy one.

Audit: read clean. The milkmaid saying is rightly hedged as attributed; the Christian Nobility paraphrase (cobbler, smith, peasant; consecrated priests and bishops by baptism) matches the 1520 text's sense. The note about 'many' is stale; the teach already says 'Lutheran and other Protestant churches'.
